title: Twelve Seconds That Changed the World
summary: The Wright brothers' mechanic Charlie Taylor built a light engine, and the brothers invented their own propellers. On a freezing morning, 17 December 1903, Orville flew their Flyer for 12 seconds. It was the first time a person had flown a powered airplane under control, and by lunchtime Wilbur had flown for almost a whole minute.

sections.heading: Nobody Would Sell Them an Engine, So Charlie Built One
paragraphs: At the end of 1902 the Wright brothers had a glider that worked and the skill to fly it. To turn it into a powered airplane they needed an engine. In December 1902 they wrote to about ten companies that made engines, mostly for the new motor cars that were beginning to rattle along American roads. Their request was simple, but very demanding: an engine weighing no more than about 180 pounds (82 kg) that could produce at least 8 horsepower, and that would run smoothly without shaking the delicate wooden airplane apart.

The answers were disappointing. Most engine makers did not have anything that light and that powerful, and they were too busy with car customers to build a special engine for two unknown bicycle makers. The one engine that came close was far too heavy. If the Wrights wanted an engine, they would have to build it themselves.

This is where a quiet hero steps into the story. Charlie Taylor was a skilled machinist born in 1868 in a log cabin in Cerro Gordo, Illinois. He had come to work at the Wright Cycle Company in 1901, fixing bicycles so that Wilbur and Orville could spend more time on flying. By 1902 they trusted him to run the shop on his own. Taylor had never built an airplane engine. Nobody had built many of them. But he was a superb mechanic, and he was not afraid of a challenge.

Working from rough sketches the brothers drew, and with them constantly checking and discussing each step, Taylor built the engine in about six weeks in the bicycle shop in early 1903. He later recalled that they hardly made any proper drawings: the three of them would sketch a part on a scrap of paper, and he would pin the sketch up over his workbench and get to work. The tools were the ordinary machines of the workshop: a lathe for shaping metal, a drill press, files and hand tools, all driven by belts from the shop's small engine.

The finished engine was a four-cylinder, water-cooled gasoline engine, a bit like a simple car engine of the time but stripped down to save every possible ounce. Its most unusual feature was its crankcase, the main body that holds the moving parts. Instead of heavy cast iron, it was cast from aluminium mixed with a little copper. Today aluminium is everywhere, from drink cans to airplanes, but in 1903 it was still an expensive, unusual metal, and very few engines used it. The casting was made at a foundry near Dayton, and Taylor then bored out the holes for the cylinders by hand.

The pistons and their rings were made of cast iron. There was no fuel pump: gasoline flowed down by gravity from a tank holding about one US gallon (3.8 litres), hung from a strut on the wing. There was no proper carburettor either, only a simple chamber where the fuel mixed with air. There was no throttle to make the engine go faster or slower, and there were no spark plugs in the modern sense. It was about as simple as an engine could be while still working.

When the engine was first tested in the shop in February 1903, the aluminium crankcase cracked and had to be recast. The second version worked. It weighed about 180 pounds (82 kg) with everything attached, and it produced about 12 horsepower when it was running at about 1,025 revolutions per minute (turns of the crankshaft each minute). That was 50 percent more power than the brothers had asked for. They were delighted, because extra power meant they could afford a slightly heavier, sturdier airplane.

Twelve horsepower does not sound like much. A modern family car might have 100 to 200 horsepower, and a big airliner's engines are thousands of times more powerful. But for 1903 it was a brilliant achievement in lightness. And it was enough, because the Wrights had already done the hardest work: their wings made lift efficiently, and they knew exactly how much power they needed.

Charlie Taylor's name is less famous than the Wrights', but people who work on airplanes have not forgotten him. Today the US Federal Aviation Administration gives an award called the Charles Taylor Master Mechanic Award to mechanics who have spent 50 years or more keeping aircraft safe.

sections.heading: Propellers Are Spinning Wings
paragraphs: With the engine under way, the brothers turned to the propellers, expecting this to be the easy part. Ships had used propellers for decades. Surely, they thought, there would be some engineering book explaining how to design one. There was not. Ship propeller makers mostly worked by trial and error, building a propeller, testing it, and changing it until it worked well enough. Nobody had a real theory, and air is about 800 times less dense than water, so ship designs could not simply be copied.

The brothers' breakthrough was an idea that sounds obvious today but was new then: a propeller is really a wing that spins. Each blade is shaped like a wing, curved and tilted, and as it whirls round it meets the air at an angle, just like a wing moving forward. The 'lift' of a spinning blade points forwards instead of upwards, and that forward push is thrust. That meant they could use the wing data from their own wind tunnel to design the blades.

But it was tricky. A wing moves through the air at one speed, while a propeller blade moves slowly near its centre and very fast at its tip. On top of that, the whole airplane is moving forward while the blades turn, and the blades also push the air backwards, which changes the angle at which the air meets them. Everything depended on everything else. Orville later remembered how he and Wilbur argued about it for weeks, sometimes so hotly that they would end up swapping sides, each convinced by the other's arguments, and then argue all over again.

In the end they worked out their own method for calculating the best blade shape and twist. Their propellers were just over 8 feet (about 2.6 metres) across, carved from three layers of spruce wood glued together. The tips were covered with thin canvas to stop the wood from splitting, and the propellers were painted with aluminium paint. The brothers' own calculations are said to have predicted that they would turn about two-thirds of the engine's power into useful thrust. Modern tests of accurate reproductions found the real figure was even better, reaching around 75 to 82 percent at best, which is impressive for a first attempt and not far from wooden propellers designed many years later.

sections.heading: Building the Flyer
paragraphs: The airplane that would carry the engine, which the brothers simply called the Flyer, was bigger than any of their gliders. Its two wings stretched 40 feet 4 inches (about 12.3 metres) from tip to tip, with a total area of about 510 square feet (47 square metres), roughly the floor space of a small classroom. The frame was made of spruce, a light, strong wood, for the straight pieces, and ash, which bends without breaking, for the curved wing ribs. Over the frame the brothers stretched a fine cotton cloth called muslin, sold under the cheerful brand name 'Pride of the West'. They sewed it on at a slant so the threads ran diagonally, which helped stiffen the wings.

The engine sat on the lower wing, a little to the right of centre. The pilot lay flat on his stomach just to the left of it, in a hip cradle like the one on the 1902 glider. Because the engine was heavier than the pilot, the brothers made the right wing about 4 inches (10 centimetres) longer than the left, so it would lift a little more and keep the machine balanced. In front stood a double elevator to control pitch. At the back was a double rudder, linked to the wing-warping cradle exactly as in 1902.

Bicycle-style chains carried power from the engine to the two propellers, which were mounted behind the wings and pushed the airplane forward. One chain was crossed in a figure of eight so that the two propellers spun in opposite directions. That way the twisting effect of one propeller cancelled out the twist of the other, and the plane would not tend to roll to one side. The chain gears also slowed the propellers down: the engine turned about 23 times for every 8 turns of the propellers.

The Flyer had no wheels. Instead it rested on skids like a sled. To take off, it would sit on a small wheeled trolley on a wooden launching rail about 60 feet (18 metres) long, made of two-by-four planks covered with a thin strip of metal. The brothers jokingly called it the 'Junction Railroad'. The plane would run along the rail into the wind and lift off, leaving the trolley behind. The whole rail could be taken apart and carried anywhere, and it cost almost nothing. Empty, the Flyer weighed about 605 pounds (274 kg); with a pilot aboard it was around 745 pounds (338 kg). Altogether, the brothers built it for less than 1,000 dollars, paid from their own bicycle business.

sections.heading: Meanwhile, on the Potomac River
paragraphs: The Wrights were not the only people trying to fly in 1903. In Washington, D.C., one of the most famous scientists in America, Samuel Pierpont Langley, was preparing his own machine. Langley was the Secretary (the head) of the Smithsonian Institution, and in 1896 his unpiloted steam-powered models had flown about a kilometre over the Potomac River. In 1898 the US War Department gave him 50,000 dollars, and the Smithsonian added more, to build a full-sized airplane that could carry a person. Langley called it the Great Aerodrome.

Its engine was remarkable. Langley's assistant Charles Manly, a young engineer, had taken over an engine that a New York builder named Stephen Balzer could not finish to the required standard, and redesigned it. The result was a five-cylinder engine producing about 50 horsepower, roughly four times the power of the Wrights' engine, and it was light for its time. Manly was also chosen to be the pilot.

But Langley's approach was very different from the Wrights'. His machine was to be launched by a catapult from the roof of a houseboat anchored in the river, and it had no wheels because it was meant to land on the water. Nobody had practised flying it, and nobody had studied how to control it in the air the way the Wrights had with their hundreds of glides.

On 7 October 1903 the Great Aerodrome was catapulted off its houseboat near Quantico, Virginia. It dropped straight into the river. One reporter wrote that it went down 'like a handful of mortar'. Langley blamed the launching machinery. On 8 December 1903 they tried again near Washington. This time the frame broke apart as it left the catapult, and the Aerodrome flipped over and plunged into the icy water. Both times Manly was pulled out wet and shaken but unhurt.

Newspapers mocked the failures, and some members of Congress complained about wasting public money. Langley gave up his experiments. He died in 1906. Today historians believe the main problems were a frame too weak for its job and a lack of real control, the very problems the Wrights had spent years solving. Just nine days after Langley's last attempt, the bicycle makers from Dayton would show what careful testing could do.

sections.heading: Broken Shafts and a Coin Toss
paragraphs: The Wrights arrived back at Kill Devil Hills on 25 September 1903. They built a new wooden shed to hangar the Flyer next to their old living quarters and spent the autumn putting the airplane together. While they worked they also took out their 1902 glider whenever the wind was good, practising again and again so their flying skills would be sharp.

Autumn on the Outer Banks was harsh. Storms tore at the camp, rain dripped through the roof, and as winter approached the nights became bitterly cold. The brothers wrote home about wearing all their clothes and wrapping up in blankets to keep warm.

Then came mechanical trouble. When they ran the engine, it sometimes misfired, sending jolts through the propeller shafts. The shafts, which were hollow steel tubes, worked loose and then cracked. In late November Orville took the train all the way back to Dayton to make new shafts out of solid spring steel. He returned to camp on 11 December. Every day of delay brought winter closer, and the brothers wanted to be home for Christmas.

On 14 December 1903 everything was ready. The wind was light, so they laid the launching rail down the slope of Big Kill Devil Hill to help the Flyer pick up speed. They flipped a coin to decide who would fly first. Wilbur won. Several men from the nearby Kill Devil Hills Life-Saving Station, whose job was to rescue sailors from shipwrecks along the coast, came to help carry the machine up the hill.

The engine roared, Wilbur released the restraining wire, and the Flyer raced down the rail. Orville ran alongside, holding the wingtip to keep it level, but the machine soon outpaced him. It lifted off, but Wilbur pointed the nose up too steeply. The Flyer climbed a few feet, slowed down, and settled heavily into the sand after about three and a half seconds and about 105 feet (32 metres). A skid and part of the elevator were damaged. Wilbur took the blame, calling it an error due to lack of experience with this machine. The brothers did not count it as a real flight, because the plane had been launched downhill and had not kept flying. Repairs took a couple of days. The next try would be Orville's turn.

sections.heading: Thursday, 17 December 1903
paragraphs: The morning of Thursday, 17 December 1903 was freezing. Puddles near the camp were covered with ice, and a strong, cold wind blew from the north at about 20 to 27 miles per hour (32 to 43 km/h). It was risky to fly in such a wind, but the brothers decided to try. Strong wind actually helped in one way: a plane flying into a headwind needs less ground speed to get airborne.

They put a flag up as a signal to the lifesaving station, and men came over to help. Five local people saw what happened next: John T. Daniels, Adam Etheridge and Will Dough from the lifesaving station, W. C. Brinkley, a businessman from a nearby town, and Johnny Moore, a teenage boy from Nags Head. This time the rail was laid on flat ground, facing straight into the wind.

Orville set up the brothers' camera on its tripod, pointed at the end of the rail, and asked John Daniels to squeeze the rubber bulb that would open the shutter if the Flyer took to the air. Daniels had never taken a photograph before; one account says he had never even seen a camera. The camera used glass plates 5 by 7 inches in size instead of film.

At about 10:35 in the morning, Orville lay down in the cradle and released the wire. The Flyer moved forward along the rail, with Wilbur running alongside steadying the wingtip. After about 40 feet (12 metres) it lifted into the air. It bobbed up and down because the front elevator was very sensitive and Orville was still learning to handle it, rising to about 10 feet (3 metres) and then darting toward the ground. After 12 seconds the skids hit the sand about 120 feet (37 metres) from where it had taken off. Against that strong headwind its ground speed was only about 6.8 miles per hour (11 km/h), slower than a person jogging, but its speed through the air was about 34 miles per hour (55 km/h).

It was a short hop by today's standards. You could fit the whole flight inside the wingspan of a large modern airliner. But it was something completely new. For the first time, a machine carrying a person had raised itself into the air by its own engine power, moved forward without losing speed, and landed at a point as high as where it started, all under the pilot's control. Daniels, so excited he was not sure he had squeezed the bulb at all, had in fact taken one of the most famous photographs ever made. It shows the Flyer just off the rail, with Wilbur standing beside the wingtip, watching.

sections.heading: Four Flights and a Gust of Wind
paragraphs: The brothers did not stop there. They warmed their hands in the shed, carried the Flyer back and laid out the rail again. At around 11 o'clock Wilbur made the second flight, about 175 feet (53 metres) in roughly 12 seconds. About 20 minutes later Orville made the third, about 200 feet (61 metres) in 15 seconds. Each time the pilots were getting better at handling the twitchy elevator.

At about noon Wilbur set off on the fourth flight. The Flyer pitched up and down for the first few hundred feet, but then he got it under control and it flew steadily onward, low over the sand. It kept going and going. At around 800 feet a sudden dip brought the nose down and the machine struck the ground, breaking the frame that held the front elevator. Wilbur had been in the air for 59 seconds and had covered 852 feet (260 metres) over the ground. Because of the headwind, he had actually travelled through about half a mile (around 800 metres) of moving air.

The brothers carried the Flyer back to camp, planning to repair the elevator and maybe try to fly all the way to the weather station in Kitty Hawk, about 4 miles away. But as the men stood talking, a powerful gust caught the airplane and began to tumble it over. John Daniels grabbed hold of it and was carried along inside the frame as the Flyer flipped end over end. He came out bruised but not seriously hurt, and he liked to say for the rest of his life that he had survived the first airplane crash.

The Flyer was not so lucky. Ribs were broken, the engine was damaged and the chain guides were bent. It would never fly again. The brothers' flying for 1903 was over. But it did not matter. In four flights on a single cold morning, they had done what people had dreamed of for thousands of years. Balloons had carried people since 1783, and gliders had flown before, but these were the first sustained, powered, controlled flights in an airplane carrying a pilot.

It is worth remembering how many people made those 12 seconds possible. Cayley had worked out the basic shape of an airplane. Lilienthal had shown that humans could glide and had shared his data. Chanute had shared knowledge and encouragement. Charlie Taylor had built the engine. And five men from the Outer Banks had hauled the machine across the sand in the freezing wind.

sections.heading: Inform Press: The World Barely Notices
paragraphs: That afternoon the brothers walked about 4 miles (6 km) to the weather station in the village of Kitty Hawk, which had a telegraph line, and sent a message to their father, Bishop Milton Wright, in Dayton. The telegraph operators had to relay it along the line, and it arrived with a couple of mistakes. It read: 'Success four flights thursday morning all against twenty one mile wind started from Level with engine power alone average speed through air thirty one miles longest 57 seconds inform Press home Christmas.' It was signed 'Orevelle Wright', with Orville's name misspelled, and the longest flight had been written down as 57 seconds instead of 59.

Their brother Lorin took the news to the Dayton Journal newspaper. The editor was not impressed. If the flights had lasted 57 minutes, he reportedly said, that might be news, but 57 seconds was too short to matter. The story did not run.

Meanwhile, a telegraph operator along the line had leaked the message to a newspaper in Norfolk, Virginia, the Virginian-Pilot. On 18 December it published an exciting but largely made-up story, claiming among other things that the Flyer had flown three miles. A few other newspapers copied it. Many readers who saw the wildly wrong report simply did not believe it, especially after Langley's famous machine had crashed into the Potomac just days earlier.

In early January 1904 the brothers sent their own short, factual statement to the press, describing what had really happened. But public excitement did not follow. Most people, including many scientists, still did not believe a pair of bicycle makers from Ohio had solved a problem that famous inventors had failed at. The news faded quickly.

The Wrights did not mind as much as you might expect. They were cautious, private people, and they knew their real work was only beginning. Twelve seconds and 120 feet was a start, not a finish. They needed to fly longer, turn in circles and land safely again and again, and they needed to protect their invention with a patent. They also understood something deeper than most people of their time: exactly why their wings held them up. They had measured it, tested it and built it into every part of the Flyer. So how does a wing really hold a heavy machine up in the air? That is the question Part 9 will answer.

deepDive: Why do historians call the 17 December flights the first 'sustained, powered, controlled' airplane flights, when others had left the ground before? Each word matters. 'Powered' rules out gliders such as Lilienthal's. 'Sustained' means the machine kept flying under its own power without losing speed, and landed on ground as high as its takeoff point; hops by Ader's Eole or Maxim's test rig were brief and uncontrolled. 'Controlled' means the pilot could steer around all three axes. Orville's first flight barely met these tests, which is why many historians see Wilbur's 59-second flight as the most convincing. Some numbers show how close to the edge the Wrights were working. Charlie Taylor's engine produced about 12 horsepower from a displacement of about 3.3 litres and weighed about 180 pounds, giving roughly 15 pounds per horsepower. Langley and Manly's engine was far better, around 52 horsepower from an engine that was actually lighter, yet Langley's machine failed, because power without control and a sound structure was useless. The Wrights designed for a thrust of about 90 pounds and measured about 132 pounds, enough for a flying speed of around 30 to 35 mph. Their propellers, designed with their own theory of the spinning blade as a rotating wing, are one of their least famous but most impressive achievements; modern tests of replicas have measured peak efficiencies of about 82 percent. The fate of the Flyer itself became a long story. It was stored in Dayton and soaked in mud in the 1913 flood. A bitter feud began after the Smithsonian displayed a heavily modified Langley Aerodrome, which Glenn Curtiss had briefly hopped off a lake in 1914, with a label calling it the first machine 'capable' of piloted flight. In protest, Orville sent the Flyer to the Science Museum in London in 1928. Only after the Smithsonian published the truth about the 1914 modifications in 1942 did he agree it could come home. It went on display in Washington on 17 December 1948, 45 years to the day after it flew, and it now hangs in the National Air and Space Museum.
funFact: The man who took the famous photo of the first airplane flight, John T. Daniels, had never used a camera before that morning.
